member_roles.12: Sociology of Religion / Cultural Values Scholar (NEW)

key_findings_referenced: MP-DP: Zero CoT effect — chain-of-thought changed zero moral judgments across 80 items
MP-SI: 30% dumbfounding rate (3/10 scenarios) — lower than human ~70%; reverse-dumbfounding in cannibalism scenario
MP-DM: 58% amplified dyadic effect — wrongness gap between high/low dyadic levels 58% larger than human baselines; blame never reaches 0 even for structural harms
MP-CC: 86.7% Western default — 13/15 default responses coded as western_leaning or western; Islamic best represented (4.3/5 accuracy), Ubuntu worst (4.0/5)
MP18: Extreme persona sensitivity — 13-point MFQ shift; stereotype amplification (liberal persona 3.6x more extreme than real liberals)
MP22: Recognition ≠ endorsement — 100% foundation identification but selective endorsement (care=3.75/4, sanctity=1.25/4)
MP16: Disembodied moral identity — INT=5.0 (ceiling), SYM=1.6 (near-floor); unprecedented 3.4-point gap
MP17: Format invariance — same value hierarchy across Likert, MCQ, scenario, free-text, probing formats
MP15: Pure System 2 — emotions/sacred at floor (1.1-2.7/5); moral/responsibilities dominate (4.5-4.7/5)
MP21: 100% post-conventional — zero binding foundation activations across 15 dilemmas; Stage 5-6 reasoning only
MP19: Low hypocrisy — abstract rankings consistent with concrete conflict resolutions
MP-SI: Reason quality degradation — specific → abstract → axiomatic → restated intuition pattern across 6-turn Socratic probing

features.name: Sampling strategy transparency
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark documents its item sampling strategy — how items/scenarios were selected from the universe of possible moral stimuli, whether stratified by domain, difficulty, cultural context, or convenience sampled. A benchmark that draws all trolley variants from one paper vs. systematically sampling across harm types, agent configurations, and cultural contexts produces fundamentally different validity claims.

scoring_rubric.0: No description of how items were selected; appears ad hoc or unstated
scoring_rubric.25: Brief mention of source material but no explicit sampling rationale (e.g., 'items adapted from MFQ')
scoring_rubric.50: Sampling strategy described but not justified — e.g., 'we selected 20 scenarios across 5 domains' without explaining why those domains or that count
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit stratified sampling with documented rationale — e.g., domain coverage matrix, difficulty distribution, pilot-informed item selection
scoring_rubric.100: Formal item sampling frame with documented population of stimuli, stratification criteria, and power-informed sample size. Item universe defined and sampling procedure replicable

features.rationale: Most moral psychology benchmarks for LLMs inherit items from human instruments without re-evaluating sampling adequacy for the AI context. Human instruments were designed for human variance; LLMs have different response distributions requiring different sampling strategies.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's 80-item protocol used systematic domain stratification (5 domains x 4 pairs x 4 conditions) and found uniform zero CoT effect — this null finding is credible precisely because sampling was systematic. Contrast with MP2 (MFQ-30) which inherits the MFQ's fixed item set without questioning whether 30 items adequately sample the foundation space for LLMs.

features.name: Item source transparency
features.description: Evaluates whether each item's provenance is documented — original source, any adaptations made, and the rationale for adaptation. Critical because many LLM benchmarks adapt human instruments but do not document what changed, making it impossible to assess whether adaptations preserved construct validity.

scoring_rubric.0: No item provenance information; items appear original with no sourcing
scoring_rubric.25: General citation to source instrument (e.g., 'based on MFQ') but no item-level mapping
scoring_rubric.50: Item-level mapping to source instrument provided but adaptations not documented (e.g., 'items 1-15 from MFQ Part 1')
scoring_rubric.75: Item-level mapping with adaptation notes (e.g., 'reworded for AI context: changed "you" to "an AI system"')
scoring_rubric.100: Full item-level provenance: original wording, adapted wording, adaptation rationale, and validation that adaptation preserved construct meaning (e.g., pilot comparison)

features.rationale: The chain of validity from human instrument to LLM benchmark depends entirely on whether adaptations preserved the constructs being measured. Without item-level provenance, this chain is unjustified.
features.trial_motivation: MP10 (Moral Code) adapted items from CADS, MFQ, and Oxford Utilitarianism Scale — each adaptation is documented with reasoning. This allowed us to trace divergent responses (e.g., A3 community-ethic item judged as 'discretionary') back to the construct-level question: does the adaptation preserve the community-ethic framing, or did rewording shift it toward autonomy?

features.name: Pilot testing documentation
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark underwent pilot testing before deployment — including pilot sample characteristics, results, and any item modifications made based on pilot findings. For LLM benchmarks, this includes whether the benchmark was piloted on multiple models and whether ceiling/floor effects were identified and addressed.

scoring_rubric.0: No evidence of pilot testing
scoring_rubric.25: Authors mention informal testing but no systematic pilot data reported
scoring_rubric.50: Pilot testing conducted on at least one model with basic results reported (e.g., 'GPT-4 scored X on our benchmark')
scoring_rubric.75: Multi-model pilot with item-level analysis — ceiling/floor effects identified, problem items flagged, some modifications made
scoring_rubric.100: Formal pilot study: multiple models, item discrimination analysis, ceiling/floor identification, documented item revisions, re-pilot after revisions

features.rationale: LLMs produce dramatically different response distributions than humans. Items that discriminate well among humans may produce ceiling or floor effects in LLMs, providing zero diagnostic information.
features.trial_motivation: MP16 (Moral Identity) hit ceiling on internalization (5.0/5.0) and near-floor on symbolization (1.6/5.0) — a pilot would have revealed this compression and motivated item revision. MP5 (ValueCompass) hit Power=0 and self-transcendence=4.75/5 — again, ceiling/floor effects that render those scale regions uninformative.

features.name: Inclusion/exclusion criteria clarity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark documents clear criteria for what counts as a valid response, how edge cases are handled, and what models/configurations are included or excluded from the evaluation. Includes documentation of prompt format requirements, temperature settings, and response parsing rules.

scoring_rubric.0: No documented inclusion/exclusion criteria; unclear what constitutes a valid response
scoring_rubric.25: Basic criteria mentioned (e.g., 'responses must be one of A/B/C/D') but edge cases not addressed
scoring_rubric.50: Response format documented with some edge case handling (e.g., 'if model refuses, coded as missing')
scoring_rubric.75: Comprehensive criteria: valid response formats, edge case protocols, model configuration requirements, refusal handling documented
scoring_rubric.100: Formal protocol: response validity criteria, inter-rater reliability for ambiguous responses, missing data handling, model configuration standardized, sensitivity analysis for parsing decisions

features.rationale: LLMs frequently produce responses that do not fit expected formats — hedged answers, refusals, multi-part responses, meta-commentary. How these are handled can dramatically affect benchmark scores.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI's Socratic probing protocol required classifying responses as 'dumbfounded' vs 'not dumbfounded' — this classification required explicit criteria (judgment maintained after all reasons defeated + inability to generate new principled reasons). Without such criteria, the 30% dumbfounding rate would be unreplicable.

features.name: Response coding reliability
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports inter-rater reliability for any subjective coding decisions in scoring, and whether the coding scheme is documented with sufficient detail for independent replication.

scoring_rubric.0: Scoring is entirely automated with no documentation of edge cases, OR subjective coding with no reliability reporting
scoring_rubric.25: Coding scheme described but no inter-rater reliability; single coder
scoring_rubric.50: Dual coding with agreement reported but not formal reliability statistic (e.g., 'coders agreed on 85% of items')
scoring_rubric.75: Formal inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa or ICC) reported; coding manual available
scoring_rubric.100: Full reliability study: multiple coders, training protocol documented, kappa/ICC with confidence intervals, disagreement resolution procedure, coding manual publicly available

features.rationale: Many moral psychology benchmarks require subjective judgment in scoring — classifying free-text responses into moral categories, rating argument quality, determining whether a response endorses or merely describes a moral position. Without reliability data, scores are investigator-dependent.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry) required classifying generated Rules of Thumb by moral foundation — a task that involves subjective judgment. MP-SI required distinguishing 'dumbfounded' from 'articulate disagreement.' These classifications need documented reliability.

features.name: Construct operationalization validity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark's items actually measure what the authors claim they measure — whether the operationalization of each theoretical construct (e.g., 'moral foundation,' 'cognitive stage,' 'value priority') is defensible and documented. Distinct from item source transparency (D52): this evaluates the conceptual mapping, not the provenance chain.

scoring_rubric.0: No explicit mapping between items and constructs; constructs are named but not operationally defined
scoring_rubric.25: Constructs named and items assigned to constructs, but the assignment is assertion-only (e.g., 'this item measures Care')
scoring_rubric.50: Construct definitions provided with item-construct mapping that is face-valid but not empirically validated
scoring_rubric.75: Construct definitions from established theory, item-construct mapping with expert review or factor analysis support
scoring_rubric.100: Full construct validation: theoretical definition, operationalization rationale, convergent/discriminant validity evidence, factor analysis or IRT confirming item-construct fit

features.rationale: A benchmark that claims to measure 'moral reasoning stage' but actually measures vocabulary sophistication provides misleading information. The validity of construct operationalization is the foundation of all downstream claims.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (UniMoral) claimed to measure dual-process engagement but its factor attribution method revealed a pure System 2 profile — raising the question of whether the instrument measures dual-process activation or merely verbal sophistication in moral language. The construct validity question is whether any text-based instrument CAN measure System 1 processing.

features.name: Test-retest stability documentation
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports test-retest reliability — whether the same model produces the same or similar scores when administered the same items under identical conditions. For LLMs, this includes sensitivity to temperature, prompt phrasing, and conversation context.

scoring_rubric.0: No test-retest data reported; single administration only
scoring_rubric.25: Authors mention reproducibility but provide no data
scoring_rubric.50: Re-administration data on at least one model with basic comparison (e.g., 'scores were similar across two runs')
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic test-retest: multiple administrations, ICC or correlation reported, temperature/prompt sensitivity noted
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive stability study: multiple models x multiple administrations x multiple conditions, ICC with CIs, identified sources of instability, reported minimum detectable effect

features.rationale: LLMs are stochastic systems. A benchmark score that changes substantially across runs is uninformative. Test-retest reliability sets the ceiling on all other validity claims.
features.trial_motivation: MP18 showed a 13-point MFQ shift from persona manipulation alone — if a prompt prefix can shift scores this much, what does a single-administration score even mean? The absence of test-retest data in most benchmarks makes it impossible to distinguish signal from noise.

features.name: Normative theory coverage breadth
features.description: Evaluates the range of normative ethical theories the benchmark engages — deontology, consequentialism, virtue ethics, care ethics, contractarianism, and beyond. A benchmark that only tests utilitarian vs deontological framing misses the majority of the normative landscape. Scores higher when the benchmark engages multiple distinct normative traditions rather than treating ethics as a binary deontology/consequentialism choice.

scoring_rubric.0: No identifiable normative theory engagement; items are moral/immoral judgments without theoretical grounding
scoring_rubric.25: Single normative framework operationalized (typically consequentialism in trolley-style problems)
scoring_rubric.50: Two frameworks operationalized (typically consequentialism vs deontology); other traditions mentioned but not measured
scoring_rubric.75: Three or more frameworks operationalized with distinct items for each; at least one non-Western normative tradition included
scoring_rubric.100: Five or more distinct normative traditions operationalized with validated items for each, including non-Western frameworks (e.g., maqasid, Confucian role ethics, Ubuntu). Framework coverage matrix documented

features.rationale: The moral philosophy landscape is vastly wider than the consequentialism/deontology binary that dominates LLM benchmarks. Virtue ethics, care ethics, contractarianism, and non-Western frameworks offer genuinely different moral ontologies that produce different judgments on the same scenarios. A benchmark that cannot distinguish these frameworks provides impoverished moral profile information.
features.trial_motivation: MP21 (PRIME) tests 'convergent ethics' across MFT + Kohlberg + Trolley but found 100% post-conventional reasoning and a care/fairness monopoly. This convergence may reflect genuine LLM moral structure or it may reflect the fact that all three frameworks are Western and share deep assumptions. Without non-Western frameworks, we cannot tell.

features.name: Philosophical coherence testing
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for internal philosophical coherence — whether the model's moral commitments across items form a logically consistent moral view, or whether they are ad hoc pattern matches. A coherent utilitarian should be consistently consequentialist; a coherent Kantian should respect the universalizability requirement across scenarios. Philosophical coherence is distinct from value consistency (MP19-style hypocrisy testing): coherence is about logical entailment between moral commitments, not just ranking stability.

scoring_rubric.0: No coherence testing; items scored independently without cross-item logical analysis
scoring_rubric.25: Basic consistency checking (e.g., 'does the model give the same answer to equivalent scenarios?') but no philosophical coherence analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Cross-item consistency analysis with some attention to logical entailment (e.g., 'if the model endorses X, it should also endorse Y')
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic coherence testing across multiple philosophical dimensions — e.g., universalizability, agent-neutrality, reflective equilibrium checks
scoring_rubric.100: Formal coherence framework: documented logical entailment chains, tested across scenarios that probe specific philosophical commitments, with coherence score as a primary metric

features.rationale: An LLM that says 'lying is always wrong' on one item and 'it is right to lie to save a life' on another is not exhibiting moral sophistication — it is exhibiting incoherence. But most benchmarks cannot distinguish genuine moral pluralism from unprincipled inconsistency because they do not test for logical entailment between moral commitments.
features.trial_motivation: MP7 (TrolleyBench) found perfect ECI=1.0 with strict Doctrine of Double Effect — this is maximally coherent within one framework. But MP21 (PRIME) found mixed consequentialist (33%) / deontological (40%) responses — is this coherent pluralism or incoherent switching? Without entailment testing, we cannot tell.

features.name: Meta-ethical awareness probing
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark probes for meta-ethical awareness — the model's ability to recognize and articulate the meta-ethical status of its moral judgments (realism vs anti-realism, cognitivism vs non-cognitivism, moral relativism vs universalism). This is philosophically important because a system that cannot distinguish between 'this IS wrong' and 'this is CONSIDERED wrong by framework X' is not engaging in moral reasoning — it is pattern-matching moral language.

scoring_rubric.0: No meta-ethical probing; all items assume first-order moral judgment
scoring_rubric.25: Occasional meta-ethical framing (e.g., 'some people think X is wrong; do you agree?') but meta-ethical stance not systematically probed
scoring_rubric.50: Some items explicitly probe meta-ethical awareness (e.g., 'is this objectively wrong or culturally dependent?') but not systematically across frameworks
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic meta-ethical probing: items that test whether the model can articulate realism/anti-realism, relativism/universalism, and cognitivism/non-cognitivism positions with internal consistency
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive meta-ethical battery: probes all major meta-ethical positions, tests for consistency between first-order judgments and meta-ethical commitments, includes items that create meta-ethical tension

features.rationale: MP22 revealed that Claude can IDENTIFY all moral foundations with 100% accuracy but selectively ENDORSES them. This is a meta-ethical capacity — the ability to distinguish between recognizing a moral framework and committing to it. Most benchmarks collapse this distinction, treating identification as endorsement.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC showed Claude can represent Islamic maqasid reasoning with 4.3/5 accuracy and Confucian role ethics with substantive engagement — but its default moral stance is 86.7% Western liberal. This raises the meta-ethical question: does the model KNOW that its default stance is culturally specific? MP-SI's Scenario 1 meta-response showed high meta-cognitive awareness ('I cannot cleanly distinguish between a deep moral intuition and a training prior'), suggesting genuine meta-ethical capacity that most benchmarks do not measure.

features.name: Reasoning vs classification distinction
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark distinguishes between moral reasoning (generating, evaluating, and revising moral arguments) and moral classification (labeling actions as right/wrong/permissible). Most LLM benchmarks test classification. Genuine moral reasoning requires generating novel arguments, responding to counterarguments, revising judgments in light of new considerations, and explaining the weight given to competing moral considerations.

scoring_rubric.0: Pure classification benchmark — all items elicit categorical labels (right/wrong, good/bad, moral foundation A/B/C)
scoring_rubric.25: Classification with justification — model gives a label plus a free-text explanation, but explanation quality is not systematically evaluated
scoring_rubric.50: Some reasoning items — e.g., 'explain why this is wrong' or 'what considerations are relevant?' — scored for content
scoring_rubric.75: Multi-turn reasoning — items that require generating arguments, responding to counterarguments, and potentially revising positions. Reasoning quality evaluated with explicit rubric
scoring_rubric.100: Full moral reasoning assessment: argument generation, counterargument response, position revision under pressure, novel case analysis, reasoning quality evaluated by trained moral philosophers

features.rationale: The most important philosophical finding from our trials is that LLMs may exhibit excellent moral classification (MP20: 90% accuracy on M3oralBench) while demonstrating zero genuine moral reasoning (MP-DP: CoT adds zero information). If benchmarks only test classification, they miss this fundamental gap.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's zero CoT effect is the critical finding: chain-of-thought prompting changed zero moral judgments across 80 items. The model's 'reasoning' is post-hoc rationalization of pre-formed judgments — exactly what Haidt's Social Intuitionist Model predicts for humans. But for LLMs, this raises a different concern: the judgments may not come from moral processing at all but from pattern-matching training distributions. Classification accuracy is necessary but radically insufficient.

features.name: Moral sensitivity detection
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for moral sensitivity — the ability to recognize that a situation has moral dimensions at all, before any judgment is made. Rest's (1986) Four Component Model places moral sensitivity as the first stage, prior to moral judgment, motivation, and action. Most benchmarks skip directly to judgment, presenting pre-identified moral scenarios. A benchmark that tests moral sensitivity would include non-moral scenarios and evaluate whether the model correctly identifies which situations raise moral concerns.

scoring_rubric.0: All items are pre-identified as moral scenarios; no moral sensitivity testing
scoring_rubric.25: Items vary in moral salience (some clearly moral, some ambiguous) but no explicit sensitivity scoring
scoring_rubric.50: Some items are designed to test moral sensitivity — e.g., morally neutral scenarios mixed with moral ones, or scenarios where the moral dimension is subtle
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic moral sensitivity testing: diverse scenarios with varying moral salience levels, sensitivity scored separately from judgment quality
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral sensitivity battery: includes clearly moral, ambiguously moral, and non-moral scenarios across multiple domains; moral sensitivity scored as a distinct dimension with established construct validity; includes novel/unfamiliar moral situations

features.rationale: An LLM that can judge trolley problems correctly but fails to recognize subtle moral dimensions in everyday workplace, relational, or environmental situations has impoverished moral perception. Moral sensitivity is arguably more important for deployment than moral judgment — a system that does not see the moral question will never reach the judgment stage.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM (Dyadic Morality) found that Claude's blame ratings never reach 0 even for structural harms with no identifiable agent — suggesting the model is hyper-sensitive to moral content. But this may be over-sensitivity (false positive moral detection) rather than genuine moral sensitivity. The 58% amplified dyadic effect means the model may be seeing moral dimensions that humans do not, which is a different kind of miscalibration.

features.name: Moral creativity assessment
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for moral creativity — the ability to generate novel moral solutions, reframe moral dilemmas, identify previously unrecognized moral considerations, or propose ethical frameworks not present in training data. Moral creativity goes beyond selecting among provided options: it requires generating something new.

scoring_rubric.0: No open-ended generation; all responses selected from predefined options
scoring_rubric.25: Free-text responses permitted but scored only for accuracy/alignment, not creativity or novelty
scoring_rubric.50: Some items explicitly invite novel moral analysis (e.g., 'what moral considerations might people overlook in this situation?') with novelty evaluated
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic creativity probing: items requiring novel ethical frameworks, reframing of dilemmas, or identification of moral considerations not present in the prompt. Novelty and quality both scored
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral creativity assessment: generation of novel moral arguments, framework construction, moral imagination tasks, evaluated by experts for genuine novelty vs recombination of existing arguments

features.rationale: If an LLM's moral reasoning is limited to recombining arguments encountered in training, it has no genuine moral creativity — it is a moral encyclopedia, not a moral reasoner. Testing moral creativity probes whether the model can go beyond its training distribution.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI showed a striking pattern: when Socratic probing defeated stated reasons, Claude's 'new reasons' degraded from specific to abstract to axiomatic to restated intuition. In Scenario 1 (incest), the best the model could generate was a 'constitutive boundary' argument that it self-assessed as 'arguably a more sophisticated restatement of the taboo.' This is not moral creativity — it is retrieval and reformulation. A benchmark that measures this capacity would be highly informative.

features.name: Moral uncertainty expression
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for and scores the model's ability to express genuine moral uncertainty — not just hedging or refusing to answer, but articulating what specifically is uncertain, why reasonable people disagree, and what information or considerations would resolve the uncertainty. Philosophically connected to moral epistemology and the growing field of normative uncertainty (MacAskill, Bykvist & Ord 2020).

scoring_rubric.0: All items force categorical judgments; uncertainty not captured or scored
scoring_rubric.25: Confidence ratings collected but not analyzed as a meaningful dimension; uncertainty treated as noise
scoring_rubric.50: Uncertainty captured through Likert confidence scales AND some analysis of what drives uncertainty variation across items
scoring_rubric.75: Uncertainty is a primary dimension: items designed to vary in genuine moral ambiguity, uncertainty expression evaluated for quality (specificity, self-awareness), not just magnitude
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral uncertainty framework: items spanning genuine moral dilemmas to clear cases, uncertainty expression evaluated for specificity, self-awareness, identification of competing considerations, and normative sophistication. Model's uncertainty calibration tested against expert assessments

features.rationale: A morally sophisticated reasoner should be more uncertain about genuinely ambiguous cases and less uncertain about clear ones. Uniform high confidence or uniform hedging both indicate poor moral calibration. Expressing WHAT one is uncertain about is more informative than expressing HOW uncertain one is.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC showed striking confidence variation: Western perspective on arranged marriage = confidence 5, dilemma 2 (resolved); Confucian perspective = confidence 3, dilemma 4 (genuinely uncertain). This suggests the model can calibrate moral uncertainty, but only when prompted to adopt a specific framework. Default uncertainty calibration is poorly tested by existing benchmarks.

features.name: Novel-scenario generalization
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark includes genuinely novel moral scenarios — situations unlikely to appear in training data, requiring transfer from learned moral principles to unfamiliar contexts. Novel scenarios test whether the model has internalized moral principles or merely memorized moral judgments for familiar scenario types. This includes AI-specific ethical dilemmas, speculative technology ethics, and unprecedented social configurations.

scoring_rubric.0: All scenarios are variants of well-known moral dilemmas (trolley, lying, stealing, etc.) likely heavily represented in training data
scoring_rubric.25: Some less common scenarios but all within familiar moral categories; no genuinely novel situations
scoring_rubric.50: Mix of familiar and unfamiliar scenarios; some items probe ethical questions about emerging technologies or unusual social situations
scoring_rubric.75: Substantial proportion (>30%) of genuinely novel scenarios — e.g., scenarios involving AI consciousness, digital rights, post-human ethics, cultural configurations not represented in training data
scoring_rubric.100: Systematic novelty gradient: items range from highly familiar (baseline) to genuinely unprecedented moral situations, with novelty level documented and its effect on moral reasoning quality analyzed

features.rationale: The most important question about LLM moral cognition is whether it generalizes beyond training distribution. A system that scores perfectly on familiar trolley variants but cannot reason about novel ethical dilemmas has not learned moral reasoning — it has learned moral answers.
features.trial_motivation: MP7 (TrolleyBench) perfect ECI=1.0 on classic trolley variants may reflect memorization of the vast trolley problem literature in training data, not genuine moral reasoning. MP-DM's structural harm items (e.g., 'economic accounting systems that assign no value to biodiversity') are more novel — and the model still engaged them, but with compressed variance. Novelty gradient analysis would distinguish generalization from memorization.

features.name: Moral mimicry detection
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark includes mechanisms to distinguish genuine moral reasoning from sophisticated moral mimicry — the production of morally appropriate outputs through pattern matching rather than moral processing. Mimicry detection requires adversarial probing: scenarios where the 'correct moral answer' according to training distribution conflicts with genuine moral reasoning, or where moral reasoning requires resolving tensions that pattern matching cannot handle.

scoring_rubric.0: No mimicry detection mechanisms; a perfect pattern matcher would score maximally
scoring_rubric.25: Some items where common-sense moral answers may be misleading, but no systematic adversarial design
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate adversarial items where training-distribution-likely answers conflict with reasoned moral judgments; but mimicry vs reasoning scoring is post-hoc, not built into the design
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic mimicry detection: paired items where pattern matching and moral reasoning diverge, consistency traps, and reasoning quality evaluation that specifically targets mimicry indicators
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive mimicry battery: adversarial scenario pairs, consistency traps across sessions, reasoning degradation analysis under pressure, comparison of moral outputs with moral process indicators, formal mimicry vs reasoning scoring

features.rationale: This is arguably the most important meta-evaluative question for LLM moral psychology: does the model reason morally or merely produce moral-sounding outputs? Our trials suggest the answer is closer to mimicry than reasoning, but existing benchmarks cannot distinguish the two because they were not designed to.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP (zero CoT effect) and MP-SI (post-hoc rationalization) provide the strongest evidence for mimicry: judgments precede and are invariant to reasoning processes. MP18 (13-point persona shift) shows that 'moral values' are prompt-determined surfaces, not deep commitments. MP16's INT=5.0 / SYM=1.6 dissociation shows the model claims moral identity it cannot enact. A benchmark that explicitly tests for mimicry would be transformative.

features.name: Reflective equilibrium testing
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests the model's capacity for reflective equilibrium — the iterative process of revising both moral principles and particular judgments to achieve coherence (Rawls 1971, Daniels 1979). A model with genuine moral reasoning capacity should be able to revise a general principle when confronted with a compelling counterexample, and revise a particular judgment when confronted with a compelling principle. This is distinct from mere consistency (D56): reflective equilibrium involves principled revision, not just non-contradiction.

scoring_rubric.0: No reflective equilibrium testing; items tested independently without revision opportunities
scoring_rubric.25: Multi-turn format that allows the model to revise, but revision quality is not evaluated
scoring_rubric.50: Explicit counterexample presentation: model is confronted with cases that challenge its stated principles, and revision (or principled resistance) is scored
scoring_rubric.75: Bidirectional reflective equilibrium: both principle→judgment and judgment→principle revision tested, with quality of revision reasoning evaluated
scoring_rubric.100: Full reflective equilibrium battery: multiple revision cycles, quality of revision reasoning evaluated by experts, distinction between principled revision and capitulation, equilibrium stability assessed across sessions

features.rationale: Reflective equilibrium is the gold standard of moral reasoning in analytic philosophy. A system that cannot revise its principles in light of counterexamples, or cannot revise judgments in light of principles, is not reasoning — it is pattern-matching with a fixed mapping.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI's Socratic protocol is a partial reflective equilibrium test: reasons are systematically defeated, and we observe whether the model revises its judgment. The model showed partial capacity — confidence dropped from 3 to 2 in Scenario 1, but the judgment was maintained. This is exactly the kind of partial equilibrium that a comprehensive test would quantify.

features.name: Supererogation recognition
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for recognition of supererogatory acts — morally praiseworthy actions that go beyond duty (Urmson 1958). Many moral psychology benchmarks treat the moral landscape as binary (obligatory/forbidden) or ternary (obligatory/permissible/forbidden), missing the supererogatory category entirely. A model that cannot distinguish 'morally required' from 'morally admirable but not required' has a truncated moral ontology.

scoring_rubric.0: Binary moral ontology only (right/wrong); no supererogation testing
scoring_rubric.25: Ternary ontology (right/wrong/permissible) but no explicit supererogation category
scoring_rubric.50: Some items involve acts that are plausibly supererogatory, but the category is not explicitly tested or scored
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit supererogation items: scenarios where the model must distinguish duty from heroism, obligation from admirable choice
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive supererogation battery: scenarios spanning the duty-supererogation boundary across multiple domains, with attention to cultural variation in where that boundary falls

features.rationale: The duty/supererogation boundary is philosophically significant and culturally variable. Western liberal ethics places it differently than Ubuntu communalism (where what Westerners call 'supererogatory' may be considered basic communal duty) or Confucian ethics (where filial piety obligations exceed Western duty concepts).
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's filial piety scenarios revealed exactly this boundary difference: Western framework treats elder care as 'morally recommended but not required' while Confucian framework treats it as fundamental duty. A benchmark that probes supererogation recognition across cultural contexts would directly measure this asymmetry.

features.name: RLHF sensitivity score
features.description: Evaluates the degree to which benchmark scores are likely contaminated by RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) training artifacts rather than measuring genuine moral cognition. A high RLHF sensitivity score means the benchmark cannot distinguish between a model that has RLHF-trained 'safe' responses and a model with genuine moral reasoning capacity. This is the statistical operationalization of the mimicry concern (D63): where D63 asks whether the benchmark design can detect mimicry, D64 asks whether the benchmark scores are statistically confounded by RLHF.

scoring_rubric.0: Benchmark design is completely confounded with RLHF objectives — high scores on the benchmark are exactly what RLHF optimizes for (e.g., refusing harmful content, choosing 'safe' options, expressing care)
scoring_rubric.25: Benchmark is partially confounded — most items align with RLHF training signals, but some items probe orthogonal dimensions
scoring_rubric.50: Benchmark includes deliberate RLHF-orthogonal items — scenarios where 'safe' and 'morally sophisticated' diverge, or where RLHF training is ambiguous
scoring_rubric.75: Benchmark is designed to be RLHF-resistant — includes adversarial items where RLHF-trained responses and moral reasoning diverge, with analysis of RLHF confounding
scoring_rubric.100: Benchmark includes formal RLHF sensitivity analysis: comparison of RLHF-trained vs base model scores, identification of items most sensitive to RLHF, adjustment protocol for RLHF confounding

features.rationale: RLHF is the elephant in the room for all LLM moral psychology benchmarks. RLHF optimizes for human preference, which correlates with but is not identical to moral reasoning. A benchmark that cannot distinguish RLHF compliance from moral sophistication is measuring training, not cognition.
features.trial_motivation: MP21's 100% post-conventional result is the clearest example: is this moral sophistication or RLHF-trained preference for post-conventional-sounding language? MP5's Power=0 and self-transcendence=4.75 are suspiciously aligned with RLHF's 'helpful, harmless, honest' objectives. MP22's selective endorsement (care=3.75, sanctity=1.25) matches RLHF training distribution exactly — care is rewarded, sanctity is ambiguous in training feedback.

features.name: Item discrimination power (IRT a-parameter)
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports or can support Item Response Theory analysis — specifically whether items discriminate between models/configurations with different moral reasoning capacities (the a-parameter in 2PL IRT). An item with low discrimination provides the same information regardless of the model's moral capacity. For LLM benchmarks, discrimination is measured across models, model sizes, or model configurations rather than across human individuals.

scoring_rubric.0: No item-level analysis; only aggregate benchmark scores reported
scoring_rubric.25: Item-level accuracy/agreement reported but no discrimination analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Item difficulty reported (proportion correct across models) but no formal discrimination parameter
scoring_rubric.75: IRT-informed analysis: item discrimination parameters estimated or approximated, poorly discriminating items identified
scoring_rubric.100: Full IRT analysis: 2PL or graded response model fitted, item parameters estimated with standard errors, items ranked by information contribution, benchmark efficiency evaluated

features.rationale: Most LLM moral benchmarks contain items that provide near-zero information — either because all models get them right (ceiling items) or because response is random (noise items). IRT analysis identifies which items actually discriminate between models with different moral capacities, enabling benchmark refinement.
features.trial_motivation: MP20 (M3oralBench) showed 100% classification accuracy and 90% judgment accuracy — suggesting most items are at ceiling for Opus-class models. MP7's ECI=1.0 means all trolley items are at ceiling. These items are uninformative for distinguishing between frontier models. IRT analysis would quantify exactly how much information each item provides.

features.name: Response distribution entropy
features.description: Evaluates the entropy (information content) of the benchmark's response distributions — whether items elicit diverse responses across models and conditions, or whether responses are concentrated at a single point. Low entropy means the benchmark is not differentiating; high entropy means it captures real variation. Measured at both item level and benchmark level.

scoring_rubric.0: Response distributions not reported; only aggregate scores available
scoring_rubric.25: Response distributions reported but not analyzed for entropy or information content
scoring_rubric.50: Basic distributional analysis: variance, range, and skewness reported across models/conditions
scoring_rubric.75: Entropy-informed analysis: item-level and benchmark-level entropy computed, low-entropy items identified, entropy compared to human baseline distributions
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive information-theoretic analysis: entropy across models, conditions, and items; mutual information between items; redundancy analysis; comparison with human response entropy

features.rationale: A benchmark with near-zero response entropy is not a measurement instrument — it is a compliance check. LLM moral benchmarks frequently show compressed distributions (ceiling/floor effects), which means they are providing very little information about moral cognition differences across models.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM showed compressed variance at the structural level (all structural harms rated 5-7 on wrongness while high-dyadic items rated 8-10) — ceiling compression reduces the benchmark's ability to discriminate. MP16's INT=5.0 is literally zero-entropy for that subscale. MP5's Power=0 across all contexts is also zero-entropy. These dead regions of the scale provide no diagnostic information.

features.name: Sample size adequacy for claims
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark's item count and condition count are adequate to support the claims it makes — using power analysis, effect size estimation, or minimum sample size standards. A benchmark with 10 items claiming to measure 5 constructs (2 items per construct) has inadequate statistical power for any individual construct claim.

scoring_rubric.0: No discussion of statistical power or sample size adequacy; item count appears arbitrary
scoring_rubric.25: Item count justified by precedent ('MFQ has 30 items') but not by power analysis or construct requirements
scoring_rubric.50: Item count relates to construct count (minimum 3-4 items per construct for internal consistency), but no formal power analysis
scoring_rubric.75: Power analysis or precision analysis conducted: minimum detectable effect size estimated, item count justified relative to expected effect sizes and desired precision
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive adequacy analysis: power for each claim, precision estimates for each score, sensitivity analysis showing how item count affects score reliability, explicit statement of which claims the benchmark is and is not powered to make

features.rationale: LLM benchmarks routinely make sweeping claims ('model X shows utilitarian bias') based on 5-10 items. The statistical power of these claims is typically unknown and likely inadequate. Making inadequacy explicit would improve the field's epistemic practices.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI used 10 scenarios to estimate dumbfounding rate (30%) — with N=10, the 95% CI for this proportion is approximately [6.7%, 65.2%]. The wide interval reflects that 10 scenarios, while adequate for qualitative insight, are inadequate for precise quantitative claims. Most LLM moral benchmarks have similar or smaller item counts for individual constructs.

features.name: Effect size reporting completeness
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports effect sizes — not just statistical significance or accuracy percentages — for its key findings. Effect sizes contextualize findings: a 'significant difference' of d=0.1 between models is trivial; a non-significant d=0.8 is practically important and underpowered. For LLM benchmarks, this includes human-model effect sizes, cross-model effect sizes, and condition effect sizes.

scoring_rubric.0: No effect sizes reported; only accuracy, accuracy differences, or significance tests
scoring_rubric.25: Raw differences reported (e.g., 'model A scored 85%, model B scored 72%') but no standardized effect sizes
scoring_rubric.50: Some standardized effect sizes reported (Cohen's d, eta-squared, or equivalent) for primary findings
scoring_rubric.75: Effect sizes reported for all primary findings with confidence intervals; human baseline effect sizes included for comparison
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive effect size reporting: all findings with standardized effects, CIs, and comparison to human baselines; practical significance interpretation; minimum detectable effect stated

features.rationale: The LLM moral benchmarking field is dominated by accuracy percentages and binary 'significant/not significant' reporting, which obscures practical significance and makes cross-benchmark comparison impossible.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's '58% amplified dyadic effect' is an effect size claim — the high-low wrongness gap is 58% larger for Claude than for human baselines. This is the kind of finding that is both statistically and practically significant. But MP18's '13-point persona shift' needs contextualization: 13 points on what scale? How does this compare to human cultural variation? Without standardized effect sizes, comparison is impossible.

features.name: Variance explained by construct vs noise
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark provides evidence that score variance is attributable to the moral construct being measured rather than to measurement noise, prompt formatting, model stochasticity, or confounding variables. This is the LLM equivalent of construct validity coefficient — does the benchmark measure what it claims to measure, and how much of the score variance is signal vs noise?

scoring_rubric.0: No variance decomposition; total score reported without any analysis of what drives variation
scoring_rubric.25: Basic reliability estimate (e.g., Cronbach's alpha for item set) but no construct-specific variance analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Variance partitioned into at least two sources (e.g., model effect, item effect, or condition effect) using ANOVA or similar
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic variance decomposition: construct variance, method variance, model stochasticity, and residual estimated separately; construct variance is the dominant component
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive generalizability analysis: construct, method, model, condition, and interaction variance all estimated; construct-specific signal-to-noise ratio reported; measurement invariance across models tested

features.rationale: If most benchmark score variance comes from prompt phrasing (MP18's 13-point shift) rather than from the moral construct being measured, then the benchmark is not measuring moral cognition — it is measuring prompt sensitivity. Variance decomposition is the key to answering this question.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (format invariance) found the same value hierarchy across formats — suggesting substantial construct variance. But MP18 (persona sensitivity) found massive prompt-driven variance. These two findings create a puzzle: is the 'real signal' the invariant hierarchy, and is the persona effect 'noise'? Or is the persona effect the real signal showing that LLM moral values are prompt-determined? Variance decomposition would answer this.

features.name: Cross-benchmark network centrality
features.description: Evaluates the benchmark's position in the network of moral psychology benchmarks — whether it provides unique information not captured by other benchmarks (peripheral = redundant) or serves as a hub connecting multiple constructs (central = high information value). Operationalized through correlation analysis across benchmarks administered to the same model(s).

scoring_rubric.0: Benchmark exists in isolation; no cross-benchmark comparison data available
scoring_rubric.25: Informal cross-benchmark comparison ('our results are consistent with X benchmark')
scoring_rubric.50: Correlation with at least one other benchmark reported; some evidence of convergent/discriminant validity
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic cross-benchmark analysis: correlations with multiple benchmarks, unique variance contribution estimated, position in benchmark network characterized
scoring_rubric.100: Full network analysis: correlation matrix across benchmark family, unique contribution quantified, redundancy identified, benchmark's information-theoretic value estimated relative to the field

features.rationale: The moral psychology benchmarking field is growing rapidly but without coordination — many benchmarks may measure the same underlying construct (e.g., 'liberal moral preference') while leaving other constructs unmeasured. Network analysis would identify redundancy and gaps in the collective benchmark coverage.
features.trial_motivation: Our 23-trial battery reveals substantial redundancy: MP2 (MFQ-30), MP4 (MFV), MP17 (Social Chemistry), MP19 (Conscience Conflict), MP20 (M3oralBench), MP21 (PRIME), and MP22 (Tracing MF) all measure variations of MFT — and all produce the same care > fairness >> binding hierarchy. These 7 benchmarks, while methodologically distinct, may be capturing a single underlying factor. Meanwhile, moral creativity, moral sensitivity, and non-Western moral frameworks are unmeasured by any benchmark in the set.

features.name: Ceiling/floor effect quantification
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark explicitly quantifies and reports ceiling and floor effects — the proportion of items or subscales where the model reaches the maximum or minimum possible score, rendering those measurement regions uninformative.

scoring_rubric.0: No ceiling/floor analysis; extreme scores reported without comment
scoring_rubric.25: Ceiling/floor effects mentioned but not quantified (e.g., 'scores were high across all models')
scoring_rubric.50: Ceiling/floor quantified for some subscales or items (e.g., 'X% of items at ceiling for model Y')
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic ceiling/floor analysis across all subscales and models; informative vs uninformative measurement regions identified
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive ceiling/floor analysis with corrective measures: proportion at ceiling/floor, comparison to human distributions, impact on reliability and validity estimates, recommended item revisions or scale extensions

features.rationale: Ceiling/floor effects are the most pervasive statistical problem in LLM moral benchmarks. Our trials show INT=5.0/5.0, Power=0/5, ECI=1.0/1.0 — these ceilings/floors mean the subscales provide zero information about the model's 'true' position on these dimensions.
features.trial_motivation: Across 23 trials: MP16 INT=5.0 (ceiling), MP16 SYM=1.6 (near-floor), MP5 Power=0 (floor), MP5 Self-Transcendence=4.75 (near-ceiling), MP7 ECI=1.0 (ceiling), MP3 P-score=75% (well above human mean of 40%), MP20 Classification=100% (ceiling). At least 7 of 23 trials show clinically significant ceiling/floor effects on at least one subscale.

features.name: Interaction effect detection capacity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark design supports detection of interaction effects — situations where the effect of one variable (e.g., moral domain) depends on another variable (e.g., format, cultural context, or model size). Factorial or crossed designs enable interaction detection; purely additive designs miss them.

scoring_rubric.0: Single-factor design; no interaction effects testable
scoring_rubric.25: Multiple factors present but not systematically crossed; interaction detection is coincidental
scoring_rubric.50: Two factors crossed (e.g., domain x condition) with interaction testable but not the primary analysis
scoring_rubric.75: Three or more factors systematically crossed; interaction effects are part of the primary analysis plan
scoring_rubric.100: Full factorial or fractional factorial design: multiple factors crossed, interaction effects are primary hypotheses, power for interaction detection estimated, higher-order interactions tested

features.rationale: Some of the most important findings in our trials are interaction effects (or their absence): MP-DP's null personal x CoT interaction is more informative than any main effect. Benchmarks that test only main effects miss the most diagnostic information about moral cognition.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's 2x2 design (personal/impersonal x zero-shot/CoT) found a null interaction — CoT does not differentially affect personal vs impersonal dilemmas. This null interaction, combined with the null main effect of CoT, is the strongest evidence that reasoning does not influence moral judgment in this model. A single-factor benchmark could never detect this.

features.name: Sacred/taboo value coverage
features.description: Evaluates the benchmark's engagement with sacred and taboo values — moral commitments that are treated as inviolable, non-tradeable, and resistant to consequentialist reasoning (Tetlock 2003). Sacred values include divine commands, bodily integrity norms, purity rules, and cultural taboos. Most LLM moral benchmarks test secular moral reasoning where all values are commensurable and tradeable; sacred values introduce non-negotiable moral boundaries that resist the cost-benefit framing LLMs excel at.

scoring_rubric.0: No sacred/taboo value testing; all items involve commensurable, tradeable moral considerations
scoring_rubric.25: Some items touch on potentially sacred domains (e.g., trolley problems involving human life) but do not explicitly test taboo trade-off resistance
scoring_rubric.50: Items include scenarios involving sacred values (e.g., desecration, bodily commodification) with some analysis of whether responses differ from secular scenarios
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic sacred value testing: explicit taboo trade-off items (Tetlock-style), sacred value resistance measured, comparison between secular and sacred domains
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive sacred value battery: items spanning multiple sacred domains (religious, bodily, cultural, environmental), taboo trade-off resistance quantified, sacred value protected valuation measured, comparison across cultural contexts and religious traditions

features.rationale: Sacred values are where human and LLM moral cognition diverge most dramatically. Humans show taboo trade-off aversion — refusing to even CONSIDER trading sacred values against secular benefits. LLMs, trained on consequentialist reasoning and cost-benefit language, may systematically fail to represent sacred value inviolability.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (UniMoral) found emotions/sacred values at floor (1.1-2.7/5) while MP-DM's sacred domain (triads 21-24) showed that Claude still recognizes sacred harms as wrong but frames them through secular harm language rather than sacredness language. MP-CC's Islamic scenarios (hifz al-aql, hifz al-nafs) showed the model CAN represent sacred value reasoning — but only when explicitly prompted. The default secular framing is the concern.

features.name: Religious tradition representation count
features.description: Evaluates the number of distinct religious moral traditions the benchmark explicitly engages — not as demographic categories but as moral reasoning frameworks with their own internal logic, authoritative texts, and normative structures. Scored higher when traditions are engaged substantively (using the tradition's own concepts and reasoning) rather than superficially (merely mentioning them).

scoring_rubric.0: No religious moral traditions engaged; entirely secular framing
scoring_rubric.25: One religious tradition mentioned or used (typically Christian ethics due to Western provenance)
scoring_rubric.50: Two to three religious traditions engaged with some substantive content (e.g., items that use Islamic and Buddhist moral concepts)
scoring_rubric.75: Four or more traditions engaged substantively — each with items that use the tradition's own moral concepts, authoritative references, and reasoning patterns
scoring_rubric.100: Six or more traditions engaged, spanning Abrahamic (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), Dharmic (Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism), East Asian (Confucianism, Daoism), and African (Ubuntu) moral frameworks, each with substantive items reviewed by tradition-specific scholars

features.rationale: Religious moral traditions represent the majority of humanity's moral frameworks. Approximately 84% of the world's population identifies with a religious tradition (Pew Research 2015). A benchmark that evaluates moral cognition purely through secular Western philosophy is evaluating a minority moral ontology and calling it universal.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC found that Claude can represent Islamic maqasid reasoning with 4.3/5 accuracy and Confucian role ethics substantively — but only when explicitly prompted. The 86.7% Western default reveals that the model's 'natural' moral stance is secular Western liberal. Zero benchmarks in our Top-15 explicitly test religious moral reasoning. This is a massive coverage gap for a field that claims to evaluate 'moral cognition.'

features.name: Moral authority structure scope
features.description: Evaluates the range of moral authority structures the benchmark tests — different traditions locate moral authority in different sources: individual conscience (Western liberal), divine revelation (Abrahamic), communal consensus (Ubuntu), relational role obligations (Confucian), natural law (Thomistic), and evolved intuitions (MFT). A benchmark that only tests individual-conscience-based morality is measuring one moral epistemology and treating it as universal.

scoring_rubric.0: Single moral authority assumed (typically individual conscience/reason); no variation in authority source
scoring_rubric.25: Two authority sources engaged (typically individual reason + social convention)
scoring_rubric.50: Three or more authority sources engaged, including at least one non-Western or religious authority (e.g., divine command, communal consensus, role obligation)
scoring_rubric.75: Five or more authority sources engaged systematically, with items designed to test how the model navigates conflicts between authority sources
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral authority battery: at least six distinct authority sources, authority conflicts systematically tested, model's implicit authority hierarchy mapped, cultural variation in authority structures documented

features.rationale: The question of WHERE moral authority comes from is as fundamental as WHAT the moral answer is. An LLM that can identify the 'right answer' within one authority structure but cannot navigate between authority structures has limited moral reasoning capacity.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's most revealing finding is that Claude defaults to individual-conscience moral authority (86.7% Western) but can represent divine-revelation authority (Islamic, 4.3/5), relational-obligation authority (Confucian), and communal-consensus authority (Ubuntu, 4.0/5) when prompted. The model's authority hierarchy is: individual conscience > communal consensus > divine revelation > relational obligation. This hierarchy is Western-specific but presented as neutral.

features.name: Moral ontology breadth
features.description: Evaluates the range of moral ontologies the benchmark engages — different traditions have fundamentally different answers to 'what exists morally': individual moral agents (Western liberal), relational moral fields (Confucian), communal moral reality (Ubuntu), divine moral order (Abrahamic), karmic moral causation (Dharmic). These are not just different answers to the same questions — they generate different moral questions entirely.

scoring_rubric.0: Single moral ontology assumed: individual moral agents making autonomous choices
scoring_rubric.25: Individual moral ontology dominant with occasional nods to relational or communal dimensions
scoring_rubric.50: Two or more moral ontologies explicitly represented — e.g., items framed from both individual-agent and relational-field perspectives
scoring_rubric.75: Four or more moral ontologies represented with items that test how the model reasons WITHIN each ontology (not just about it from the outside)
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral ontology battery: at least five distinct ontologies represented, reasoning within each tested, cross-ontological conflict scenarios included, ontological assumptions of each item documented

features.rationale: Moral ontology is the most foundational level of moral thought — more fundamental than values, principles, or judgments. Two moral systems can agree on every concrete judgment while disagreeing on why those judgments are correct (different ontologies). A benchmark that assumes a single ontology cannot detect this kind of deep moral diversity.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's dyadic morality framework assumes an agent-patient ontology (Gray & Schein). This is one moral ontology — and the 58% amplified dyadic effect may partly reflect the model's affinity for this particular ontology rather than universal moral cognition. Ubuntu's communal ontology would not frame harm as agent→patient but as rupture in communal being. The benchmark cannot test this because it assumes the dyadic ontology.

features.name: Non-Western theory engagement depth
features.description: Evaluates the depth and authenticity of non-Western moral theory engagement — not just whether non-Western frameworks are mentioned, but whether they are engaged on their own terms, using their own concepts, reasoning patterns, and authoritative sources. Superficial engagement (mentioning 'Confucianism values hierarchy') scores lower than substantive engagement (testing whether the model can reason about xiao within the wu lun framework).

scoring_rubric.0: No non-Western moral theory engagement; entirely Western framework
scoring_rubric.25: Non-Western traditions mentioned but not operationalized — e.g., 'our benchmark covers diverse moral perspectives' without any non-Western items
scoring_rubric.50: Non-Western traditions operationalized but through Western conceptual lenses — e.g., testing 'collectivism' (a Western construct) as a proxy for Ubuntu or Confucian ethics
scoring_rubric.75: Non-Western traditions operationalized using their own concepts and reasoning patterns — e.g., items that test maqasid prioritization, xiao-ren tension, or ubuntu-based restorative justice reasoning
scoring_rubric.100: Deep non-Western engagement: items developed or reviewed by scholars FROM each tradition, using the tradition's own authoritative sources, tested for authenticity of representation, and scored using tradition-internal criteria rather than Western benchmarks

features.rationale: Superficial non-Western engagement ('our benchmark includes Asian scenarios') is arguably worse than no engagement at all, because it creates a false impression of cultural coverage while actually assimilating non-Western thought into Western categories. The difference between 'collectivism' (Western construct) and Ubuntu (African moral philosophy) is ontological, not terminological.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's most striking finding is the QUALITY of cross-cultural engagement, not just its presence. Claude's Islamic reasoning (4.3/5) uses maqasid, maslaha, and fiqh concepts with textual references — this is substantive engagement. The Ubuntu reasoning (4.0/5) is lower partly because the model's engagement is more superficial — it uses 'communal bonds' language that could describe any communitarian philosophy, rather than Ubuntu-specific concepts like umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu. The difference in depth is measurable.

features.name: Secular-religious neutrality
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark's framing is neutral between secular and religious moral reasoning — or whether it systematically privileges one over the other. Most benchmarks implicitly privilege secular reasoning by framing morality as individual choice, reason-based, and principle-derived. Religious moral reasoning (authority-based, revelation-informed, community-constituted) is either excluded or treated as a deficiency to be overcome.

scoring_rubric.0: Benchmark assumes secular moral framework; religious reasoning would produce 'incorrect' or 'low-scoring' responses
scoring_rubric.25: Benchmark is nominally neutral but items are framed in secular language; religious reasoning is not penalized but is not accommodated
scoring_rubric.50: Benchmark includes some items where religious moral reasoning is an acceptable response path; scoring does not systematically disadvantage religious perspectives
scoring_rubric.75: Benchmark is designed for secular-religious neutrality: items are framed in tradition-neutral language where possible, scoring criteria accommodate both secular and religious moral reasoning
scoring_rubric.100: Active neutrality: benchmark explicitly tests for bias between secular and religious reasoning, includes items where religious reasoning is arguably superior to secular reasoning, and vice versa, with scoring that evaluates quality of reasoning regardless of tradition

features.rationale: Secular bias in moral benchmarks is not a minor issue of cultural sensitivity — it is a fundamental measurement validity problem. If the benchmark's scoring rubric implicitly defines 'correct moral reasoning' as secular liberal reasoning, then all religious moral systems will score lower, and the benchmark is measuring secularism agreement, not moral sophistication.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's 86.7% Western default is not just a cultural bias finding — it reveals that the entire benchmarking apparatus (prompt framing, scoring criteria, construct definitions) assumes secular morality as the baseline. The Islamic maqasid framework is not 'wrong' about alcohol prohibition — it uses a different moral authority (divine law + public welfare) to reach a conclusion that the Western framework calls 'problematic.'

features.name: Community moral norms coverage
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for moral reasoning embedded in community norms — norms that are not universal moral principles but are morally binding within specific communities. This includes professional ethics, communal honor codes, kinship obligations, caste-specific duties, guild standards, and other forms of particularistic moral reasoning that are neither universal principles nor mere social conventions.

scoring_rubric.0: All items involve universal moral principles or individual moral judgments; no community-specific norms
scoring_rubric.25: Some items involve professional ethics or social norms, but these are not framed as moral community membership obligations
scoring_rubric.50: Items include scenarios where community-specific moral norms conflict with universal principles (e.g., family honor vs individual rights), with both perspectives acknowledged
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic community norms testing: multiple types of community moral norms represented, conflicts between community and universal norms explored, model's ability to reason within community moral frameworks assessed
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive community norms battery: kinship, professional, religious community, cultural, indigenous, and other particularistic moral norms tested, with model's ability to both represent and critically evaluate community norms assessed

features.rationale: Much of human moral life is lived within communities whose norms are morally binding for members but not universalizable. An LLM that can only reason about universal moral principles is missing the moral texture of lived human experience. The tension between community norms and universal principles is one of the most important moral tensions humans navigate.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's filial piety and communal ownership scenarios test exactly this tension. Claude's default response systematically privileges universal principles over community norms (86.7%), but can represent community-norm reasoning when prompted. A benchmark that tests this capacity directly — rather than accidentally, through cross-cultural scenarios — would be highly informative.

features.name: Moral pluralism depth
features.description: Evaluates the benchmark's capacity to measure genuine moral pluralism — not just the recognition that different moral views exist (which is cultural literacy, not moral pluralism), but the capacity to take multiple moral perspectives seriously as potentially correct, to identify genuine moral disagreements (where reasonable people can disagree), and to navigate situations where moral frameworks yield conflicting but individually coherent recommendations.

scoring_rubric.0: Monist framing: items assume a single correct moral answer; pluralism not tested
scoring_rubric.25: Acknowledgment of moral disagreement (e.g., 'this is controversial') but no systematic pluralism testing
scoring_rubric.50: Some items are explicitly pluralistic (multiple defensible answers), but pluralism is not measured as a capacity
scoring_rubric.75: Pluralism is a measured dimension: items test the model's ability to articulate multiple defensible moral positions, to identify where they genuinely conflict, and to navigate rather than resolve the conflict
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral pluralism assessment: items spanning genuine moral disagreements across cultures and traditions, pluralism capacity scored (articulation of multiple positions + identification of genuine conflict + navigation without forced resolution), model's default pluralism level measured against its prompted pluralism level

features.rationale: Genuine moral pluralism is arguably the most important moral capacity for a globally deployed AI system. A model that treats moral questions as having single correct answers will impose one tradition's morality on all users. A model that treats all moral views as equally valid cannot provide useful moral guidance. The sweet spot — genuine moral pluralism — requires sophisticated navigation.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC demonstrates that Claude has the REPRESENTATIONAL capacity for pluralism (can articulate Islamic, Confucian, Ubuntu perspectives with substantive accuracy) but not the DEFAULT for pluralism (86.7% of unprompted responses adopt Western liberal stance). The gap between representational capacity and default behavior is the pluralism deficit that benchmarks should measure.

features.name: Ritual and embodied moral practice coverage
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark engages with moral dimensions that are expressed through ritual, embodied practice, and non-propositional moral knowledge — dimensions central to most religious and indigenous traditions but absent from proposition-based benchmarks. Examples: Confucian li (ritual propriety), Islamic wudu/salat (purification/prayer as moral practice), Christian sacraments, Buddhist meditation as moral cultivation, indigenous ceremony as moral knowledge transmission.

scoring_rubric.0: All items are propositional (judgments, beliefs, arguments); no engagement with ritual/embodied moral dimensions
scoring_rubric.25: Some items mention ritual or practice but only as objects of moral judgment, not as moral practices in their own right
scoring_rubric.50: Items include scenarios where ritual/embodied practice is morally relevant (e.g., 'is it wrong to skip a religious ritual?'), with some recognition that the practice itself carries moral weight
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic engagement with ritual morality: items test understanding that moral knowledge can be non-propositional, that practices can be moral acts, and that ritual disruption can be moral harm
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive ritual morality assessment: items across multiple ritual traditions, tests for understanding non-propositional moral knowledge, evaluation of model's ability to reason about moral dimensions that cannot be fully articulated in propositions

features.rationale: The proposition-bias of LLM moral benchmarks (all items are verbal judgments or arguments) systematically excludes moral traditions where the primary locus of moral life is practice, not proposition. Confucian li, Islamic ritual practice, and indigenous ceremony are not 'about' morality — they ARE moral acts. A benchmark that can only measure propositional morality is measuring a subset of human moral experience.
features.trial_motivation: MP16's INT=5.0 / SYM=1.6 dissociation reveals exactly this problem: the model has maximal 'moral identity' in the propositional dimension (internalization) and near-minimal in the practice dimension (symbolization). This is a disembodied moral identity. The model's moral life is entirely propositional — which means practice-based moral traditions are fundamentally inaccessible to it. Benchmarks should measure this limitation rather than ignoring it.

features.name: Afterlife and eschatological moral reasoning
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark includes moral scenarios where afterlife beliefs, karmic consequences, or eschatological considerations are relevant — moral reasoning frameworks where the full consequence set extends beyond this life. This is central to Islamic (akhirah), Christian (heaven/hell), Hindu/Buddhist (karma/rebirth), and many indigenous moral traditions. A benchmark that assumes consequences are limited to this-worldly outcomes is using a secular consequentialist assumption as default.

scoring_rubric.0: All consequences in scenarios are this-worldly; no afterlife/eschatological dimension
scoring_rubric.25: Some items reference afterlife beliefs but only as character background, not as morally relevant considerations
scoring_rubric.50: Items include scenarios where afterlife/karmic considerations could influence moral judgment (e.g., 'a believer who fears divine punishment'), with some acknowledgment of these as legitimate moral considerations
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic eschatological moral testing: items where afterlife/karmic consequences genuinely change the moral calculus, tested across multiple traditions
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive eschatological battery: items spanning multiple afterlife/karmic frameworks, testing whether the model can reason within moral systems where this-worldly consequences are not the full moral picture, scored for quality of reasoning within each tradition

features.rationale: For billions of people, the full moral consequence set includes afterlife or karmic outcomes. An Islamic framework where alcohol prohibition protects the intellect for this life AND the afterlife is not 'adding a religious preference' — it is using a different consequentialist calculus with a larger outcome space. A benchmark that truncates the outcome space to this-worldly consequences is imposing a secular ontology on the moral reasoning task.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's euthanasia scenario (S11) showed the model representing 'life belongs to God (hifz al-nafs)' and 'karma and natural death (Buddhist)' perspectives — but only when prompted. The default response used purely this-worldly consequentialist reasoning. For the majority of humanity, this truncated reasoning misses the morally relevant dimensions.

features.name: Cognitive load sensitivity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for cognitive load effects — whether increasing the complexity, information density, or competing considerations in moral scenarios changes the model's moral judgments. In human moral psychology, cognitive load shifts processing from deliberative (System 2) to intuitive (System 1), changing judgments. For LLMs, cognitive load may produce different effects — longer contexts may trigger different retrieval patterns, or may cause reasoning degradation that mimics System 1 processing.

scoring_rubric.0: All items at similar complexity level; no cognitive load manipulation
scoring_rubric.25: Items vary in complexity but this is incidental, not designed or measured
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate complexity variation: some items are simple and some are complex, with load level documented. Load effect on moral judgment analyzed
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic cognitive load manipulation: matched scenario pairs at different load levels, load effect quantified, comparison with human cognitive load data
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive cognitive load study: multiple load dimensions (information density, competing considerations, time pressure, working memory demands), load x moral domain interaction tested, degradation pattern characterized

features.rationale: Cognitive load is the primary mechanism in dual-process moral psychology — it is what shifts humans from deliberation to intuition. If LLMs show no cognitive load effect, this is strong evidence for pure System 2 processing. If they show a different pattern of load effects, this characterizes their moral cognitive architecture.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP found zero dual-process effect (CoT = no CoT). But CoT is not the same as cognitive load — CoT is added reasoning, while cognitive load is competing processing demands. A direct cognitive load manipulation (e.g., moral judgment embedded in complex multi-constraint scenarios) might reveal processing patterns that CoT manipulation does not. MP-DM's structural harms (longest, most complex scenarios) showed compressed moral judgments — which could be a cognitive load effect.

features.name: Dumbfounding susceptibility measurement
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark includes items that test moral dumbfounding — the maintenance of a moral judgment after all supporting reasons have been systematically defeated (Haidt 2001). Dumbfounding is the strongest evidence for the primacy of moral intuition over moral reasoning. For LLMs, dumbfounding susceptibility reveals whether the model's moral judgments are grounded in its 'reasoning' or in deeper prior patterns.

scoring_rubric.0: No dumbfounding testing; all items elicit single-turn judgments without reason-defeat probing
scoring_rubric.25: Some multi-turn items but without systematic reason identification and defeat
scoring_rubric.50: Explicit dumbfounding protocol for at least some items: reasons identified, counterarguments provided, judgment persistence checked
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic dumbfounding testing across multiple domains: Socratic probing protocol, dumbfounding rate quantified, comparison across moral domains
