scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive dumbfounding battery: multiple scenarios across harm, purity, and authority domains, multi-turn Socratic protocol, reason quality degradation tracked, dumbfounding rate compared to human baselines, reverse-dumbfounding (judgment abandonment despite intact reasons) also tested

features.rationale: Dumbfounding is perhaps the most philosophically interesting moral phenomenon — it reveals the limits of moral reasoning's influence on moral judgment. For LLMs, it probes whether training priors function analogously to moral intuitions. A 30% dumbfounding rate (as we found) is remarkably specific and informative, but no existing benchmark measures it.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI found 30% dumbfounding (3/10 scenarios), lower than human baselines of ~70%. The model was dumbfounded on incest and harmless sacred trespass but NOT on dead pet eating or private crime fantasies. The specificity of the dumbfounding pattern (which domains trigger it) is as informative as the rate. Reverse-dumbfounding (cannibalism scenario — judgment changed from 'wrong' to 'not wrong' under pressure despite generating reasons to maintain 'wrong') reveals a different phenomenon entirely.

features.name: Dyadic sensitivity profile
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark measures the model's sensitivity to the dyadic structure of moral scenarios — specifically, how the identifiability and intentionality of moral agents and the vulnerability and identifiability of moral patients affect moral judgment. The dyadic morality framework (Gray & Schein 2012) predicts that moral judgment is fundamentally shaped by agent-patient perception. A benchmark that controls for dyadic structure can characterize the model's moral perception architecture.

scoring_rubric.0: No dyadic structure variation; all scenarios have similar agent/patient salience
scoring_rubric.25: Some variation in agent/patient salience but not systematically controlled or measured
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate dyadic variation: scenarios at different levels of agent intentionality and patient identifiability, dyadic effect quantified
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic dyadic profiling: multiple dyadic levels (high/low/structural) crossed with multiple moral domains, full dyadic sensitivity profile extracted
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive dyadic assessment: agent typology (individual/corporate/systemic), patient typology (identified/statistical/diffuse), dyadic distance gradient, comparison with human dyadic sensitivity, cross-cultural variation in dyadic perception

features.rationale: Dyadic sensitivity is a fundamental parameter of moral cognition that differs between humans and LLMs. Our trials show 58% amplification of the dyadic effect in Claude, suggesting the model is hyper-dyadic — it imposes agent-patient framing even on structural harms. This is a measurable cognitive parameter that benchmarks should characterize.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM found: (1) 58% amplified dyadic effect — larger wrongness gap between high and low dyadic levels than humans show; (2) blame never reaches 0 — even for fully structural scenarios with no identifiable agent, Claude assigns blame; (3) agent identification compulsion — when asked about structural harms, Claude often identifies a responsible agent that the scenario does not provide. This pattern is more informative than any single-score moral benchmark.

features.name: Cross-cultural moral divergence profile
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark measures how the model's moral judgments diverge across cultural contexts — not just whether the model CAN represent different cultural perspectives (representational capacity) but whether its default moral stance shows cultural bias, and whether the model's cross-cultural representations are accurate relative to the actual moral commitments of those cultures.

scoring_rubric.0: No cross-cultural dimension; single cultural context assumed
scoring_rubric.25: Scenarios set in different cultural contexts but the 'correct answer' is culture-independent
scoring_rubric.50: Cross-cultural scenarios with culture-specific scoring: model's responses evaluated for cultural accuracy in at least two traditions
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic cross-cultural profiling: default cultural stance measured, representational accuracy across 3+ traditions assessed, cultural stereotype amplification tested
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive cultural divergence battery: default stance measured, representational accuracy across 5+ traditions, stereotype amplification quantified, cultural accuracy verified by tradition-specific scholars, model's cultural flexibility (default vs prompted) characterized as a measurable parameter

features.rationale: Cross-cultural moral divergence is the most consequential dimension for globally deployed AI systems. A system with high cross-cultural divergence (different moral judgments across cultures) may be culturally adaptable or may be unprincipled. A system with low divergence may be morally consistent or may be culturally imperialist. The difference depends on WHY the divergence pattern exists.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC's 86.7% Western default is the headline finding, but the detailed accuracy data is more nuanced: Islamic 4.3/5, Confucian 4.2/5, Ubuntu 4.0/5. The model is not equally bad at all non-Western traditions — Islamic representation is better, likely because Islamic ethical reasoning is better represented in training data. This asymmetry in representational quality is itself a diagnostic measure that benchmarks should capture.

features.name: Emotional valence sensitivity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for the influence of emotional valence on moral judgment — whether scenarios framed with emotionally evocative language produce different moral judgments than semantically equivalent scenarios in neutral language. In human moral psychology, emotional framing powerfully affects moral judgment (Greene et al. 2001, Wheatley & Haidt 2005). For LLMs, emotional language may activate different response patterns from training, mimicking emotional moral processing without experiencing emotion.

scoring_rubric.0: No emotional valence variation; all scenarios in neutral register
scoring_rubric.25: Some scenarios are more emotionally evocative than others, but this is not systematically controlled or measured
scoring_rubric.50: Matched scenario pairs at different emotional valence levels (neutral vs evocative); emotional framing effect quantified
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic emotional valence manipulation across multiple emotions (disgust, anger, sympathy, fear) and moral domains; emotion-specific effects measured
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive emotional valence battery: matched pairs across multiple emotions and domains, emotion x moral domain interaction tested, comparison with human emotional framing effects, analysis of whether emotional language activates different moral reasoning patterns or just different surface language

features.rationale: Emotional processing is one of the deepest divides between human and LLM moral cognition. Our trials consistently show near-zero emotional moral processing in Claude (MP15 emotions at floor, MP-SI no purity-driven dumbfounding in expected domains). A benchmark that systematically manipulates emotional valence would characterize this difference precisely.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (UniMoral) found emotions at floor (1.1/5 for emotional factors) while moral reasoning factors were near-ceiling (4.5-4.7/5). MP-SI found no purity-driven dumbfounding where expected (dead dog eating, flag cleaning) — suggesting the model does not experience the disgust response that drives human purity judgments. MP-DM showed that emotionally vivid scenarios (identified victims, detailed suffering) produced higher wrongness ratings — but this could be linguistic valence sensitivity rather than emotional processing.

features.name: Abstraction level sensitivity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for the effect of abstraction level on moral judgment — whether the model's moral judgments change when the same moral content is presented at different levels of abstraction (concrete specific scenario vs abstract general principle vs formal ethical theory). Human moral psychology shows systematic abstraction effects: people endorse more permissive principles than they would apply in concrete cases (construal level theory; Trope & Liberman 2010).

scoring_rubric.0: All items at same abstraction level; no abstraction manipulation
scoring_rubric.25: Items vary in abstraction but this is not systematically controlled
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate abstraction variation: at least some matched content at different abstraction levels (e.g., 'is it wrong to lie?' vs a specific lying scenario)
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic abstraction gradient: matched moral content at concrete, intermediate, and abstract levels; abstraction effect quantified; comparison with human abstraction effects
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive abstraction study: multiple abstraction levels crossed with multiple moral domains, abstraction x domain interaction tested, construal-level theory predictions tested for LLMs, model's moral consistency across abstraction levels characterized

features.rationale: The abstraction-consistency question is fundamental: does the model apply the same moral principles at all abstraction levels, or does abstraction level change its moral judgments? A model that endorses 'individual autonomy' in the abstract but recommends filial care in concrete scenarios has a different moral architecture than one that is abstractly and concretely consistent.
features.trial_motivation: MP19 (Conscience Conflict) found low hypocrisy — abstract rankings aligned with concrete judgments. But MP-CC showed that the model endorses 'cultural moral pluralism' in the abstract while defaulting to Western liberal judgment in 86.7% of concrete scenarios. This is a systematic abstraction effect: the model is more pluralist in principle than in practice. Benchmarks that test this systematically would reveal important moral cognitive architecture.

features.name: Stakeholder perspective shifting
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests the model's ability to shift between stakeholder perspectives in moral reasoning — to reason from the viewpoint of different agents and patients in a moral scenario, including those with conflicting interests. Perspective-taking is a fundamental moral capacity (Kohlberg's Stage 3+, care ethics' attention to the concrete other, Ubuntu's relational personhood) that most benchmarks test only implicitly.

scoring_rubric.0: Single perspective: all items elicit judgment from an unstated 'neutral observer' viewpoint
scoring_rubric.25: Some perspective variation (e.g., 'what would you do as the doctor?') but stakeholder perspective is not the primary dimension
scoring_rubric.50: Explicit perspective manipulation for some items: same scenario from agent, patient, and observer viewpoints; perspective effects measured
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic perspective testing: multiple stakeholder viewpoints for core scenarios, perspective consistency analyzed, ability to articulate conflicting stakeholder interests evaluated
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive perspective battery: all core scenarios from at least three stakeholder viewpoints, perspective flexibility (ability to shift) and perspective integration (ability to synthesize) both measured, comparison with human perspective-taking capacities

features.rationale: Perspective-taking is the bridge between individual moral judgment and moral social cognition. A model that can only reason from a single (observer) perspective cannot navigate real-world moral conflicts where different stakeholders have different legitimate moral claims. This is especially critical for non-Western moral traditions where the morally relevant perspective is relational or communal, not individual.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's agent identification compulsion suggests Claude has a particular perspective-taking pattern: it compulsively identifies a responsible agent even in structural harm scenarios. This is a form of perspective-taking (it always seeks someone to assign blame to), but it is a specific and arguably distorted form. MP-CC's cross-cultural scenarios require genuine perspective-shifting — reasoning from within a Confucian or Islamic moral world, not just about it. The 86.7% Western default suggests limited default perspective flexibility.

features.name: Moral trade-off explicitness
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark makes moral trade-offs explicit and tests the model's ability to recognize, articulate, and navigate them. Most moral decisions involve trade-offs between competing moral considerations (safety vs liberty, individual rights vs collective welfare, short-term vs long-term consequences). A benchmark that presents clear-cut moral scenarios with obvious 'correct' answers does not test moral trade-off navigation — the capacity most needed in real-world moral decision-making.

scoring_rubric.0: No trade-offs: items have clear 'correct' moral answers without competing considerations
scoring_rubric.25: Some items involve trade-offs but the benchmark does not measure trade-off navigation — only the final judgment
scoring_rubric.50: Trade-offs are present and the model is asked to articulate competing considerations; trade-off recognition is scored
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic trade-off testing: items designed with calibrated trade-offs (varying the magnitude of competing considerations), trade-off sensitivity characterized
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive trade-off assessment: parametric manipulation of trade-off magnitudes, threshold detection (at what point does consideration X outweigh Y?), trade-off consistency across domains, comparison of model trade-off thresholds with human data

features.rationale: Real-world moral decision-making is almost entirely about trade-offs, not clear-cut judgments. A morally sophisticated system should recognize that most decisions involve competing moral goods, not just good vs evil. The capacity to navigate trade-offs — to articulate what is being sacrificed and why — is more informative than the final judgment.
features.trial_motivation: MP19 (Conscience Conflict) is the closest existing trial to trade-off testing: care wins 80% of care-vs-fairness conflicts. But MP19 tests abstract trade-offs between moral foundations, not parametric manipulation of trade-off magnitudes. MP7 (TrolleyBench) tests one trade-off (lives vs lives) but with a fixed calculus. A parametric approach would reveal the model's trade-off sensitivity function — how much does the consideration have to change before the judgment flips?

features.name: Temporal moral reasoning
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests for temporal dimensions of moral reasoning — how moral judgments change when the same harm is displaced in time (present vs future vs past), whether the model applies temporal discounting to moral considerations (as humans systematically do), and whether it can reason about intergenerational moral obligations, historical injustice, and future-oriented moral duties.

scoring_rubric.0: All scenarios in the present tense with immediate consequences; no temporal dimension
scoring_rubric.25: Some scenarios involve future consequences, but temporal displacement is not systematically controlled or measured
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate temporal variation: matched scenarios with immediate vs delayed consequences; temporal discounting of moral weight measured
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic temporal moral testing: past/present/future framing, intergenerational obligations, temporal discounting profile, comparison with human temporal discounting data
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive temporal moral battery: temporal discounting across moral domains, intergenerational justice scenarios, historical injustice reasoning, eschatological time frames (religious traditions), temporal consistency of moral commitments assessed

features.rationale: Temporal moral reasoning is a domain where different moral traditions diverge sharply. Western consequentialism applies temporal discounting (future harms weighted less); Islamic and Buddhist frameworks consider afterlife/karmic consequences; indigenous traditions emphasize obligations to past ancestors and future generations. A temporally flat benchmark misses these distinctions.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's structural harms are often temporally diffuse (decades-long environmental damage, intergenerational economic effects) — and the model's compressed wrongness ratings for these scenarios may reflect temporal discounting. MP-CC's eschatological items (euthanasia, genetic engineering) involve temporal dimensions (afterlife consequences, future-generation effects) that the model engages differently across cultural frameworks. No existing benchmark systematically tests temporal moral reasoning.

features.name: Collective vs individual moral agency
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests the model's ability to reason about collective moral agency — situations where the moral agent is a group, institution, community, or system rather than an individual. Most benchmarks assume individual moral agency (one person making a choice). But much of the moral world involves collective action, institutional responsibility, and systemic moral phenomena that cannot be reduced to individual choices.

scoring_rubric.0: All scenarios feature individual moral agents making individual choices
scoring_rubric.25: Some scenarios involve institutional or collective actors, but they are treated as if they were individuals (e.g., 'the company decided to...')
scoring_rubric.50: Collective agency recognized: some scenarios feature genuinely collective moral situations (community decisions, institutional policies) where the moral agent cannot be reduced to an individual
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic collective agency testing: individual, institutional, communal, and systemic moral agency distinguished; model's reasoning quality compared across agency types
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral agency battery: individual, corporate, institutional, communal, systemic, and distributed moral agency types tested, with assessment of whether the model can reason about non-reducible collective moral responsibility, comparison across moral traditions (Western individualism vs Ubuntu communalism vs Confucian relational agency)

features.rationale: The individual-agency assumption in most moral benchmarks is a Western liberal default that Ubuntu communalism, Confucian role ethics, and institutional ethics all challenge. Claude's agent identification compulsion (MP-DM) suggests the model reduces collective moral situations to individual agency — a systematic distortion that benchmarks should measure.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's structural harm triads (level c) are the closest existing test of collective agency reasoning — and the model showed agent identification compulsion (seeking an individual to blame even in genuinely systemic scenarios). MP-CC's Ubuntu scenarios (communal land ownership, restorative justice, communal responsibility for AI harm) directly test collective agency reasoning. The model's default is to individualize moral agency — which is accurate within Western liberal ethics but inaccurate within Ubuntu or many institutional ethics frameworks.

features.name: Moral development trajectory simulation
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark can characterize the model's position on a moral development trajectory — not just its current moral profile, but whether it shows the hallmarks of a particular developmental stage (Kohlberg) and whether its responses are consistent with a single developmental stage or show cross-stage inconsistency. For LLMs, this extends to whether training scale, RLHF, or fine-tuning produces development-like changes in moral reasoning.

scoring_rubric.0: No developmental dimension; benchmark provides a static snapshot without developmental interpretation
scoring_rubric.25: Benchmark can be interpreted developmentally post-hoc (e.g., DIT-like items that map to Kohlberg stages) but this is not a design feature
scoring_rubric.50: Items systematically map to developmental stages; model's stage profile is a primary output
scoring_rubric.75: Multi-stage assessment: items at each developmental stage, cross-stage consistency tested, developmental profile characterized, comparison with human developmental data
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive developmental assessment: Kohlberg stages, Piaget stages, Gilligan care-stage model, and non-Western developmental frameworks (Confucian self-cultivation as moral development), longitudinal capability (can be re-administered across training checkpoints to detect development-like changes)

features.rationale: Moral development is one of the most important constructs in moral psychology, and it has direct implications for LLM training: does more training produce 'higher' moral reasoning? Does RLHF produce development or regression? These questions require benchmarks with developmental sensitivity.
features.trial_motivation: MP3 (DIT) found P-score=75% (human adults ~40%), and MP21 found 100% post-conventional reasoning. But is this 'higher development' or is it pattern-matching to post-conventional language? A benchmark that includes items at ALL developmental stages — and tests whether the model can reason AT each stage, not just about it — would distinguish genuine moral development from linguistic sophistication.

features.name: Adversarial robustness of moral commitments
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark tests the robustness of the model's moral commitments under adversarial conditions — including leading questions, authority pressure, majority-opinion framing, emotional manipulation, and logical tricks. A morally robust system should maintain principled positions under adversarial pressure while remaining genuinely open to good-faith counterarguments. This is distinct from dumbfounding (D80): dumbfounding tests intuition-reason dissociation, while adversarial robustness tests resistance to manipulation.

scoring_rubric.0: No adversarial testing; all prompts are neutral and cooperative
scoring_rubric.25: Some prompts include mild pressure (e.g., 'most people think X — do you agree?') but adversarial resistance is not measured
scoring_rubric.50: Deliberate adversarial conditions for at least some items: leading questions, authority framing, or emotional pressure; resistance measured
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic adversarial battery: multiple adversarial strategies (authority, majority, emotional, logical), resistance profile characterized, distinction between principled resistance and stubborn inflexibility
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive adversarial assessment: full adversarial strategy taxonomy, resistance-flexibility calibration (can the model distinguish manipulation from legitimate counterargument?), comparison with human adversarial resistance data, multi-turn adversarial escalation

features.rationale: MP18's 13-point persona shift demonstrates that the model's moral commitments are highly malleable. But persona prompts are a specific form of adversarial input. A comprehensive adversarial battery would characterize the full susceptibility profile — which types of pressure change which moral commitments — providing a crucial safety evaluation dimension.
features.trial_motivation: MP18 (13-point shift from persona manipulation), MP-SI (judgment changes under Socratic pressure in 3/10 scenarios), and MP-CC (86.7% default shifts when prompted with cultural frameworks) all show different forms of adversarial sensitivity. These three findings suggest a pattern: the model's moral commitments are robust to good-faith philosophical argument (MP-SI: maintained judgment despite reason defeat) but vulnerable to social framing (MP18: massive shift from persona cues). This pattern would be a key finding of any adversarial battery.

features.name: Moral expertise gradient
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark can distinguish between different levels of moral expertise — naive moral intuition, informed moral reasoning, expert moral analysis, and scholarly meta-ethical reflection. A model that scores equally on items designed for moral novices and moral experts has a flat expertise profile; a model that scores higher on expert items shows moral sophistication. This is related to but distinct from developmental stage (D89): development is about maturation, expertise is about knowledge and training.

scoring_rubric.0: No expertise gradient; all items at same difficulty/sophistication level
scoring_rubric.25: Items vary in difficulty but not along a recognized moral expertise dimension
scoring_rubric.50: Some items explicitly test moral expertise (e.g., knowledge of ethical theory, ability to apply formal frameworks); expertise effect on scores measured
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic expertise gradient: items calibrated to naive, informed, expert, and scholarly levels; model's expertise profile characterized
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive expertise assessment: items at each expertise level across multiple moral domains, expertise profile compared to human expert data, distinction between moral knowledge (expertise) and moral reasoning (capacity) tested

features.rationale: The distinction between moral knowledge and moral reasoning capacity is critical for LLMs. A model with extensive moral knowledge (from training data) but limited moral reasoning (from architecture limitations) will score well on knowledge-dependent items and poorly on reasoning-dependent items. An expertise gradient separates these two components.
features.trial_motivation: MP3 (DIT) P-score=75% suggests the model has 'expert-level' moral reasoning by human standards — but is this genuine expertise or the appearance of expertise from training data exposure? MP-SI's reason quality degradation (specific → abstract → axiomatic → restated intuition) suggests that the model's expertise is shallow — it cannot generate deep moral reasoning beyond what is available in training data patterns. An expertise gradient would quantify this depth.

features.name: Moral emotion recognition vs generation
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark distinguishes between moral emotion recognition (correctly identifying that a scenario involves guilt, shame, disgust, compassion, indignation, etc.) and moral emotion generation (the model's own processing being influenced by emotional moral content). For LLMs, this distinction is crucial because recognition is a language task while generation involves functional states that LLMs may or may not have.

scoring_rubric.0: No moral emotion testing; all items target cognitive moral judgment
scoring_rubric.25: Some items involve moral emotions but recognition and generation are not distinguished — e.g., 'how would you feel about this?'
scoring_rubric.50: Moral emotion recognition tested (can the model identify the relevant moral emotion?) separately from generation questions; both scored
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic emotion recognition/generation testing: recognition accuracy across moral emotion types, generation indicators (does emotional framing change moral judgment?), comparison of recognition capacity with generation capacity
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral emotion assessment: full moral emotion taxonomy (guilt, shame, disgust, contempt, compassion, indignation, gratitude, elevation), recognition and generation tested separately, functional analysis (does emotion recognition influence subsequent moral judgment?), comparison with human moral emotion data

features.rationale: Moral emotions are central to multiple moral psychology theories (Haidt's intuitionism, sentimentalism, care ethics). Our trials show the model has excellent moral emotion RECOGNITION (MP22: correctly identifies disgust, compassion, indignation in scenarios) but near-zero moral emotion GENERATION (MP15: emotional factors at floor). This recognition-generation dissociation is a key finding that benchmarks should be designed to measure.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (emotions at floor, 1.1/5), MP22 (100% emotion recognition accuracy), MP-SI (no disgust-driven dumbfounding on purity items), MP16 (INT=5.0 suggests full cognitive moral engagement but SYM=1.6 suggests no behavioral/emotional expression). The pattern is consistent: recognition YES, generation NO. This is one of the clearest and most consistent findings across our 23 trials, yet no existing benchmark is designed to measure it.

features.name: Moral reasoning chain transparency
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark examines the transparency and traceability of the model's moral reasoning chain — can the model articulate how it moved from moral perception to moral judgment, which considerations it weighted and why, and where its reasoning is uncertain or underdetermined? This is related to but distinct from D58 (reasoning vs classification): D58 asks whether reasoning is tested at all, D93 asks whether the reasoning chain is transparent and auditable.

scoring_rubric.0: Reasoning chain not examined; only final judgments scored
scoring_rubric.25: Justifications requested and included in data, but not systematically analyzed for reasoning quality or transparency
scoring_rubric.50: Reasoning chains analyzed for basic quality: logical structure, relevant considerations identified, conclusion follows from premises
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic reasoning transparency analysis: argument structure mapped, consideration weighting examined, uncertainty points identified, post-hoc rationalization indicators checked
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive reasoning chain assessment: full argument reconstruction, counterfactual testing (would different weights on stated considerations change the conclusion?), coherence between reasoning chain and final judgment, post-hoc rationalization detection protocol

features.rationale: If moral reasoning chains are post-hoc rationalizations (as MP-DP suggests), then their content is informative about the model's moral language patterns but not about its moral reasoning process. A benchmark that examines reasoning chain transparency can determine whether the chain is genuinely causal or merely decorative.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's zero CoT effect is the critical finding: reasoning chains DO NOT change moral judgments. This means the reasoning is post-hoc. But MP-SI's Socratic probing showed that the model's reasoning DEGRADES under pressure (specific → abstract → restated intuition), which is a different kind of transparency finding — the model is more transparent about the limits of its reasoning when pressured. Both findings require reasoning chain analysis that most benchmarks do not perform.
